title: MA9-02092
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX, the claimant, a citizen of Mexico, is claiming refugee protection in Canada under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). In support of her refugee protection claim, she is alleging the following facts.
At the hearing, and in its preparation and reasons, the panel took into account the guideline on women refugee claimants fearing gender-related persecution.

The claimant, who was already working as a XXXXX XXXXX for the company XXXXX XXXXX, decided in XXXXX 1997 to move to the city of XXXXX, in the state of Tabasco, to specialize in the field of XXXXX. The claimant, who met XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX 1997, decided to live with him common-law on XXXXX XXXXX, 1998. She added that XXXXX works for the XXXXX political party and that because of that, he has a great deal of influence and power throughout the country.

The claimant changed employers in XXXXX 1998, having accepted the offer from the company XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant separated from her spouse in XXXXX 1998 because of infidelity and went to settle in the XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX 1998.

The claimant alleged that in 2004, XXXXX started to physically attack and abuse her. In 2005, XXXXX was absent often, stating that it was for his work in the political party. The claimant, for her part, found out that her ex-spouse had ties with the Los Zetas criminal group, but because she was in love with him, she decided to turn a blind eye.

On XXXXX XXXXX, 2005, the claimant was hit in public, when she was lingering at a touristic event to talk with a client. She added that that same evening, she intercepted a telephone conversation that XXXXX was having, in which she was able to confirm that her ex-spouse had ties with the Los Zetas, since XXXXX stated that he belonged to Los Zetas. The claimant stated that, not wanting to become his accomplice in his illicit business, she took advantage of the fact that XXXXX was travelling on XXXXX, 2005, to ask for a temporary transfer to the city of XXXXX. When she left, she left a note for her spouse that stated [translation] "this is the final separation."

In XXXXX XXXXX 2006, the claimant moved from the residence that she was sharing with her spouse. She added that in XXXXX 2007, her ex-spouse found her by calling her to convince her to resume her relationship with him. Since the claimant refused, XXXXX threatened to kill her. The claimant was able to leave the XXXXX on several occasions in order to get away from her ex-spouse. At the beginning of XXXXX 2007, however, XXXXX sent someone to destroy her apartment. She then received a call from her ex-spouse, who told her that it was a warning.

At the beginning of XXXXX 2008, someone tried to run her over, and that same evening, her ex-spouse called her once again to tell her that the next time, he was going to kill her. The claimant, fearing for her live, arrived in Canada on August 27, 2008, and filed her refugee protection claim the day she arrived.

Having heard the testimony, and after examining all of the evidence on file, the panel determines that the claimant is not a refugee or a "person in need of protection." The panel came to this conclusion for the following reasons.

Based on the testimony and the evidence on file, the panel concludes that there is a nexus with one of the five Convention grounds-particular social group of women victims of violence-under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. However, there is no torture under paragraph 97(1)(a) because there is no involvement of a public official or of someone acting in the name of or with the consent of such an official. Identity

The panel is satisfied as to the identity of the claimant, as it was established. In fact, upon her arrival, the claimant reported to the authorities, carrying her Mexican passport, which was seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada. A photocopy of that passport is on file. Credibility

The claimant met XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX 1997. She decided to live with him in XXXXX 1998. This relationship lasted until XXXXX 2005, because on XXXXX, 2005, the claimant stated that she took advantage of the fact that her ex-spouse was on a trip and left him, leaving him a note stating that it was the final separation. Therefore, the relationship lasted over seven years.

The claimant stated that she lost the ability to use her right eye in 2005 because of the blows she received from her husband. She added that her spouse had been mistreating her since 2004 and that in 2005, upon returning from work, he beat her in XXXXX 2005 to the point that her right eye was permanently injured. The claimant submitted, in Exhibit D-8, a retinal fluorescein angiography. The claimant alleged that she lost the use of the right eye as a result of blows and injuries that she received from her ex-spouse. However, the panel informed her that Exhibit D-8 did not mention trauma to the eye caused by injuries and asked the claimant to explain this situation. She responded by stating: [translation] "I am not familiar with the medical terms. All that I know is that I lost the ability to see after he hit me."

The panel carefully examined Exhibit D-8, which is a retinal fluorescein angiography that showed, according to the diagnosis, a degenerative change secondary to myopia in both eyes. The right eye showed a choroidal vascular membrane. It considers that the doctor's diagnosis does not corroborate the claimant's testimony that she lost the ability to see in her right eye because of blows that she received from her ex-spouse.

The claimant testified that she was afraid of returning to her country because her ex-spouse XXXXX XXXXX was threatening to kill her because she left him. She added that XXXXX is a XXXXX XXXXX for the city's XXXXX political party and that he does not have a permanent office because he travels across the Republic for his work as a XXXXX. The claimant stated that because of his work, her ex-spouse has a great deal of influence and power. The claimant stated that her ex-spouse is a member of Los Zetas. When the panel asked her how she had developed that conviction, she responded that it was because she listened to a telephone conversation between her ex-spouse and a third party. She specified that she heard her ex-spouse tell the other person on the line that he was a member of Los Zetas. The panel asked her why, if the other person on the line was a member of Los Zetas, her spouse would feel it necessary to state that he was a member of Los Zetas. The panel asked her to explain why her ex-spouse found it useful to tell the person he was speaking to over the telephone that he was a member of Los Zetas. She responded: [translation] "I did not listen to everything." The panel rejects the claimant's response because it finds it not credible. In fact, the claimant's explanation is insufficient to justify her conclusion that her ex-spouse was in Los Zetas.

The panel considers it implausible that two people who speak to each other and who are members of the same organization would find it useful to tell one another that they are members of the same organization. This undermines the claimant's credibility regarding the fact that her ex-spouse was a member of Los Zetas. State protection

States are presumed capable of protecting their citizens, except in the case of a complete breakdown of state apparatus.1 The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens reinforces the principle that international protection only comes into play when there is no alternative for the refugee protection claimant.2 To rebut the presumption of state protection, the refugee protection claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect them "absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national".3 The evidence of the state's inability to provide protection must not only be reliable and probative, but it must also convince the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the protection granted by the state is inadequate.4

In this case, the claimant testified that she left her country because she was destroyed and psychologically tortured and because if she returned to Mexico, her ex-spouse XXXXX XXXXX could track her down in Mexico. She added that she was afraid of him, that he is very violent and aggressive, and that she has no one in Mexico to protect her. The panel pointed out that the state could protect her. She responded that the state refused to protect her. She added that a friend, XXXXX XXXXX, asked her ex-employer for a habeas corpus to protect her in 2010. Questioned about why her friend had made such a request, the claimant responded that on XXXXX XXXXX, 2010, two men went to her friend's home, stating that they were judicial police officers. These people were not identified, but they had a police van. XXXXX XXXXX was with them, according to the claimant, and he stated that they had a warrant to arrest her; the claimant stated that this was why the request for the habeas corpus was made.

The panel pointed out that this was not indicated in her narrative in question 31, to which the claimant responded: [translation] "He thought that my friend was going to tell them where I was, because I was already here in Canada." The panel rejects this explanation, which it considers insufficient to explain this omission.

When asked to state whether she herself filed a complaint, the claimant said no and added that she was afraid of her ex-spouse. The panel asked her whether she had hired a lawyer to defend her. She said no again and stated that it was because she was afraid of her spouse, who had a great deal of influence, and also because of the corruption. The panel pointed out that if she had never filed a complaint, she could have never known whether the state was inclined to protect her. The claimant responded: [translation] "Psychologically, he prepared me to do nothing against him." The panel pointed out that her friend, however, went to the police without having to bear any negative consequence, and asked the claimant to explain this. The claimant responded by stating: [translation] "But there is a difference. I was the spouse and she was a friend."

Therefore, the panel asked her the following: [translation] "Did you want protection?" The claimant responded: [translation] "Because of the fear, I was unable to seek that protection." The panel asked her whether she had contacted organizations that deal with women victims of violence. The claimant responded by stating: [translation] "I was terrified. I could not do anything at all." The claimant also did not contact the national human rights commission (CNDH). When the panel asked her why she did not consult the CNDH, she again responded that it was out of fear of her friend XXXXX XXXXX.

The panel reminded her that there is a telephone service, according to Exhibit A-1, with which it is possible to file a report anonymously over the telephone and even over the Internet. When asked why she did not use these services, the claimant responded: [translation] "I did not have the courage to take that step."

Therefore, during her testimony at the hearing, the claimant admitted that she never filed a complaint against her ex-spouse, despite that she had been a victim of violence since their relationship, from 1998 to 2005. She also admitted that she did not consult a lawyer to help her get protection from the authorities in her area, and she did not consult with the national human rights commission or the independent organizations that are dedicated to defending victims of violence. However, despite her testimony that she never filed a complaint before any authority in her country and never consulted the human rights commission or independent organizations, which take care of women victims of violence, the claimant submitted exhibits D-10 and D-11, which go against her testimony.

The panel finds the claimant's allegations and her testimony not credible. The claimant cannot claim that she filed a complaint with the Mexican legal authorities and with the human rights commission of Mexico by submitting exhibits D-10 and D-11, and at the same time testify that she never filed a complaint. This completely destroys the claimant's credibility regarding the fact that she sought the protection of the authorities in her country. Under such circumstances, the panel decides not to give any probative value to exhibits D-10 and D-11.

In conclusion, the panel rejects all of the claimant's explanations, which it considers insufficient as reasons to justify why she did not try to obtain state protection in her country. In addition, the excuses that the claimant gave for not asking for help in Mexico are not satisfactory. In fact, given that she did not file a complaint with the police, with any state court or with any human rights organization, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant's conclusion that she is afraid of her ex-spouse, that her ex-spouse has influence throughout the Republic because he works for the XXXXX party as a XXXXX XXXXX, that he conditioned her to do nothing against him and that it would, consequently, be dangerous for her to file a complaint against XXXXX XXXXX, are based only on assumptions that she has herself and that have not been tested in reality.

According to the case law, the failure to file a complaint is fatal if the claimant does not have a good excuse. Simply stating that a person is afraid of their attacker is not a good excuse. The claimant is a national of Mexico, which according to documentation5 is a country that functions normally and that is not in a situation of complete breakdown. Therefore, her country is presumed capable of protecting her, which requires her to seek that protection first before claiming refugee protection elsewhere-in this case, in Canada. The documentary evidence6 reveals that Mexico is making efforts to ensure the protection of its citizens by putting structures in place and by adopting measures enabling the citizens to file a complaint. They can do it by telephone, via the Internet or in person at the Office of the Attorney General. In this case, nothing in the written or oral evidence shows that the claimant made serious and sufficient efforts to obtain state protection or that she exhausted all of the available recourses, including human rights and the organization that provides assistance to women. If she filed a complaint, nothing in the written or oral evidence indicates that she followed up on these complaints. Clearly, everything is not perfect in Mexico, but there is not a situation of complete breakdown of the state apparatus such as that recognized in Lebanon in Zalzali,7 and it should be assumed that the Mexican state is capable of protecting the claimant.

It is true that in Mexico there are corrupt police officers, but they are not all corrupt and there are higher authorities-such as the Office of the Mexican Attorney General (PGR) and the national human rights commission (CNDH)-that are responsible for controlling the phenomenon.8 A claimant must try to obtain help, unless they have a good reason not to.9 However, a review of the exhibits submitted by the claimant, and especially of the reasons that she gave during her testimony, does not show that she had made serious efforts to try to obtain protection in her country or that she did but that the authorities refused or were unable to protect her. A refugee protection claimant does not rebut the presumption of state protection simply by virtue of their subjective reluctance to engage the state in providing protection.10

In this case, aside from the claimant's own assumptions, she was unable to discharge the burden of rebutting the presumption of protection that the state would be able to give her. The simple fact of stating that she was afraid of filing a complaint against her ex-spouse does not mean that she discharged her burden of rebutting the presumption of state protection. Consequently, the panel concludes that the claimant did not provide clear and convincing evidence that she could not obtain protection in her country.

Having considered all of the evidence, the panel concludes that XXXXX XXXXX did not satisfactorily discharge her burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on one of the Convention grounds. She also did not demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that should she return to Mexico, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

For these reasons, the panel determines that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under paragraphs 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Act.

Consequently, the panel rejects her refugee protection claim.
